# Daniel Arcé
Daniel Arcé — Senior Front-End Developer & Design Technologist in Toronto. Production interfaces, accessibility, and working prototypes for media products, photo archives, and image tools.

## About
Hello, I’m Daniel Arcé.

I’m a senior front-end developer and design technologist based in Toronto. Most of my professional work has been in front-end development: building production interfaces, making them usable from the keyboard, and working out interaction decisions in code. At MSNBC, I held the Senior Design Technologist and Front-End Developer role; today I also design and build independent applications.

### From prototype to production interface

A working prototype gives a team something to try. A selection leads to another view; that view may expose a choice that was easy to miss in a static screen. Trying the interaction helps us decide what to keep, what to change, and what the implementation needs to support.

I stay involved as those decisions reach production. My front-end work includes React and TypeScript, with keyboard interaction and focus management built into the behaviour of the interface.

At Catch (August 2024–February 2025), I built production React and TypeScript interfaces, including API and authentication integration and Cypress tests.

At [PhotoShelter](/projects/photoshelter/), I led a WCAG audit and front-end remediation, including custom keyboard behaviour across Polymer, Web Components, and Shadow DOM. I mentored four developers on accessible patterns. Working with the Chief Architect, I also built a workflow-automation prototype that exposed integration issues and informed Smart Galleries.

At [MSNBC](/projects/msnbc/), I proposed and prototyped collapsible panels so viewers could browse coverage and read comments while the video continued playing. I helped deliver the resulting AngularJS interface with the internal team and vendors within a six-month launch window. At [Apple](/projects/apple/), I implemented responsive launch pages from the marketing and design team’s specifications and automated campaign build and preview steps.

### Building around photographs and film

For [Texting Syria](/projects/texting-syria/), photographer Liam Maloney supplied the photographs, text, and translations; I developed the experience end to end. The exhibition connected photographs with actual messages delivered to visitors’ phones through an SMS server.

My recent image applications extend that practice into search and description. [Visual Search Workbench](/projects/visual-search-workbench/) is a macOS app I designed, built, and released. Start with words or a picture, choose a promising image, then follow related photographs through a map and linked grid. Its bundled models process photographs on the Mac; my documented checks include an 8 GB Apple Silicon machine.

[AltContext](/projects/altcontext/) is still in development. It uses a photograph, a publisher’s named people roster, and page context to draft descriptions in WordPress. The editor reviews face suggestions and wording before applying the text. I build the React/TypeScript interface, WordPress PHP integration, and Python services. Evaluation with editors and blind readers remains to be done.

### Keeping decisions available during development

AI-assisted development introduced another problem into my practice: decisions and review findings could be lost between coding sessions. I built [WorkBay](/projects/workbay/) to preserve those records outside the conversation and retrieve them in a later session, including when I move to another supported coding tool. I use different agents for orchestration, implementation, and review so that work can be checked without inheriting the author’s conversation.

I also use UX maps to inventory interfaces and examine proposed changes. Those maps can be rendered as text screens and flows for people and AI tools to review. [Heuristics Canon](/research/heuristics-canon/), a collection I maintain, supplies specific questions and references for the critique. I check the resulting changes in the running interface.

### Get in touch

I’m interested in senior front-end development and design-technology roles, with production interface work at their centre. I’m based in Toronto and open to New York City.

[Email me](mailto:daniel.arce@gmail.com) about a role or a project.

Portrait by Liam Maloney.

## Projects

### Visual Search Workbench
*Find a picture, then follow its visual neighbours*
Year: 2026
Tags: Interaction Design, Visual Search, UMAP, SwiftUI, Core ML, macOS Development
Summary: Designed and built a SwiftUI app for searching photo folders and following visual neighbours, with linked UMAP, Places, and Timeline views and local Core ML processing.
I designed and built Visual Search Workbench in SwiftUI with local model processing. Release 0.2.6 is available for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs.

I built Visual Search Workbench around the point where finding a photograph turns into following a visual idea. A search may begin with something specific, then return a picture that suggests another direction. I wanted that picture to become the next query without making someone invent a new description for it.

The app searches photographs in folders you choose. You can start with words or a reference image, inspect the results, and use a promising photograph to find related pictures. Explore adds a similarity map linked to an image grid, with Places and Timeline views for examining the same selection by location or date.

![A search for flowers returns photographs from a film-scan collection, with a selected image open for inspection.](/images/work/sis-search-layer.png)

*These application captures show version 0.2.0, under the earlier name Semantic Image Search. The downloadable release documented here is 0.2.6.*

### Give the search a starting point

I keep the search index separate from the original photographs. The app reads the folders you select and leaves the files where they are. Its image representations let a query follow what a picture depicts even when the filename is only a camera number; you do not have to tag the collection first.

A text query is useful when you can describe what you remember. A reference image is useful when the quality you are looking for is easier to show. You can drop a picture into the app or choose **Find similar** on one already in the collection.

When a photograph becomes the query, a banner names the reference. **Back to text results** returns to the earlier search. Those controls make the change of query visible and give it a way back, so following one image does not require starting over.

![A flower photograph is named as the reference for Find similar, above the resulting images.](/images/work/sis-similarity-search.png)

A search for flowers, for example, might turn up a picture worth following for its colour. That photograph can then lead to references that would have been difficult to request with the original search terms.

### Explore the collection on a map

I used UMAP for the **Similarity** view. It takes the images’ numerical representations and looks for a two-dimensional arrangement that keeps neighbours near each other. This gives the collection regions to explore instead of presenting every result in one ranked list.

The map is linked to the grid. Select a region and the photographs behind it appear below, where you can judge the images themselves and choose one to follow. That connection is important: the layout offers an overview, but the photographs are still what the person needs to inspect.

![A Similarity map of a 2,314-photo collection, with photographs from a selected region shown in the grid.](/images/work/sis-layers-umap.png)

*Selecting a region connects the overview to the photographs it contains.*

The regions are not automatically named categories, and distances on the map are not exact measurements of visual difference. [Finding a Visual Direction with UMAP](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/) develops the design idea; the [interaction reference](/research/visual-search-workbench-screen-reference/) follows the individual views and controls.

### Look at the selection by place or time

A selection carries between **Similarity**, **Places**, and **Timeline**. Places uses recorded coordinates, while Timeline lets you examine wider or narrower periods. Each view retains its zoom and pan when you change tabs. Selecting a photograph opens the available metadata, including camera information, capture time, and location.

I also worked on what happens while that information is loading. In release 0.2.6, the plot and timeline appear before all dates and locations have been read, then fill in as the metadata arrives. An unfinished metadata read no longer has to hold back the whole view.

The time slider needed a related correction. A request made earlier can finish after a newer one. I changed the handling so the selection and results settle on the range most recently requested, including after a drag or a change of time axis. An older response cannot replace the range the person has just chosen.

The same release fixed a preview crash caused by the people-name reader misinterpreting a metadata value in photographs from some cameras. It also made same-named folders distinguishable by their paths and corrected a count’s singular and plural forms on screen and in VoiceOver. The [release notes](https://github.com/darce/visual-search-workbench/releases/tag/v0.2.6) document these changes.

### Take a cutout into another project

Search can lead to a photograph whose subject would be useful in a composition. I added an experimental cutout feature that proposes subject layers with transparent backgrounds. The layers can be inspected and saved for use elsewhere.

![A cat photograph with proposed cutout layers, each marked experimental.](/images/work/sis-cat-layers-detail.png)

The proposed separation still needs judgment. An edge can be rough or a label can be wrong. Cutouts remain a secondary experiment alongside the search and exploration work.

### Keep the work on the Mac

I built the macOS interface in SwiftUI and use Core ML for local model processing. The app bundles its search and cutout models, so it does not need to fetch them at first launch. The photographs are processed on the Mac; my network checks found no gallery data leaving the device in the tested flows.

My documented checks include an 8 GB Apple Silicon Mac. Larger-library performance and peak memory still need measurement. I have not yet run an outside-user study to test whether the app helps people find remembered images or develop useful references for a creative brief.

### Download

[Download Visual Search Workbench 0.2.6](https://dl.darce.xyz/) for Apple Silicon or Intel, macOS 14 or later.

The app is not notarized by Apple, so macOS may block its first launch. The [release instructions](https://github.com/darce/visual-search-workbench/releases/tag/v0.2.6) explain the opening procedure. The [GitHub repository](https://github.com/darce/visual-search-workbench) distributes the built app, model-licence information, and checksums; it does not publish the application source.

### AltContext
*Use the photograph, confirmed identities, and page context to draft image descriptions*
Year: 2026
Tags: Interaction Design, Accessibility, React, TypeScript, WordPress, PHP, Python, FastAPI
Summary: Developing a React interface, WordPress integration, and Python services that combine photographs, confirmed identities, and page context for editor-reviewed image descriptions.
I am designing and developing AltContext’s React interface, WordPress integration, and supporting recognition and description services. The product is in development.

A description such as “a person singing on a stage” can explain an activity while leaving out who is pictured. On a page about a particular performer, that identity may be important to understanding why the photograph is there.

I am building AltContext to bring that publishing context into WordPress image descriptions. The product combines the photograph with a site’s own people roster and information from the page. An editor reviews the proposed identity and the wording before applying the text. The intended benefit is more useful context for blind readers; establishing that benefit with readers is still part of the work ahead.

### What supports the draft description

The photograph supplies visual information: a microphone, clothing, or something else visible in the scene. An image model can describe those details without having to identify the person from its general knowledge.

Names come from the publisher’s roster. In WordPress, an editor associates groups of faces with people and corrects mistaken groupings. A face in a new photograph can then be compared with those site-specific references. The result is a proposed match for review. The naming policy also determines whether a name may be used in the generated text.

The page supplies a different kind of information. A caption or surrounding paragraph can explain why the publisher chose an image and which details matter. A performer’s identity may be relevant to an event report, while an article about a garment may need more attention to the clothing. [W3C’s image guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/) describes how purpose and context shape an image’s text alternative.

I keep those sources distinct in the drafting workflow. Mentioning a person in an article does not establish that the person appears in its photograph. The reconciliation step separates visual observations from page or event context before drafting, so background information is not presented as something the image shows.

### Review the proposal before applying it

The editor first needs enough information to judge the proposed identity. The workflow lets them compare the image with reference photographs and decide whether the person should be named. That decision informs the description, which can then be edited before it is saved.

I separate generation from applying the text. A generated draft is a proposal in the interface; it does not become a stored WordPress description simply because the service returned it. The editor can change the wording or decline a suggested name before applying the result.

The workflow also supports a longer description alongside alt text. Decorative images can skip generation and use an empty text alternative. The interface needs to accommodate those publishing decisions alongside the review of generated descriptions.

### Connect the interface to the stored decision

I am responsible for the interaction design and the implementation behind it. The admin interface uses React and TypeScript, with PHP for the WordPress integration and Python/FastAPI for the supporting services. Working across those parts lets me follow an editorial action from the control on screen to the record it changes.

The service is designed around tenant-scoped recognition data and API isolation between publishers. I use task briefs and acceptance tests to define the work, and code review as part of the versioned delivery process. An interface change has to be considered alongside the WordPress integration and supporting service it uses.

I also use [WorkBay’s UX-map workflow](/projects/workbay/#review-the-interface-as-well-as-the-code) to inventory an existing interface or examine a proposed change. The resulting screens and flows can be reviewed by people and AI tools, and findings can be checked in the running interface after implementation. This supports review of structure and behaviour; it does not replace evaluation with editors and readers.

### Try the decisions in a practice copy

The [public practice guide](https://demo.altcontext.com/guide/) uses names and descriptions prepared in advance from a recorded run. Recognition is not running while someone uses the guide.

For each photograph, choose whether to use the suggested names or leave the people unnamed. Once both choices have been made, the prepared description appears in an editable textarea. **Use this description** changes the demo image’s alt text. **Keep the current description** leaves it as it is, and **Undo this change** restores the original.

The guide does not require sign-in. Its changes affect only the demo image on that page, clear on reload, and do not publish to WordPress.

### Make the processing and retention choices explicit

AltContext uses a WordPress host and a hosted processing service. WordPress remains the source of record for names, editorial corrections, and saved descriptions. Recognition and description processing run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, so images leave the WordPress host for that work. The hosted service also stores the recognition representations used for face comparison.

Recognition data is retained by default unless another retention mode is selected. The hosted records have retention settings and export and purge operations, with controls for withholding names from generated text. Export and purge operations leave an audit trail.

Purging hosted recognition data does not erase saved WordPress descriptions or that audit trail. Saved descriptions also remain available when a new service request cannot run. These are separate records with different lifetimes, and the controls have not undergone a legal compliance assessment.

### Evaluate the description and the review

Model comparisons have examined whether supplied identities survive into the text and whether page context introduces unsupported claims. Automated checks cover the plugin and services, including accessibility checks on the admin interface. The implementation has not had an independent security audit.

Evaluation with blind readers and editors is still needed. Readers need descriptions that preserve useful context. Editors need to recognise plausible mistakes in a proposed match or a fluent draft and correct them before publication. Those are the outcomes that will establish whether the workflow is useful.

### PhotoShelter: Production Accessibility & Workflow Prototypes
*Keyboard interaction, reusable patterns, and product prototyping*
Year: 2022
Tags: Front-End Development, Accessibility, Web Components, React, Mocha, Jenkins, Interaction Prototyping, OpenCV.js
Summary: Led production accessibility work at PhotoShelter, built keyboard behaviour across Web Components and Shadow DOM, maintained Mocha tests, and developed React workflow prototypes with the Chief Architect and UX team.
I led PhotoShelter’s WCAG 2.1 audit and front-end remediation, including keyboard interaction across Web Components. I also mentored four developers and built exploratory prototypes with the Chief Architect and UX team.

### Keyboard access across the production interface

PhotoShelter’s digital asset management platform served more than 80,000 users and hosted over a billion files at the time of this work. Its core menus needed keyboard support. A person who could operate a control with a mouse could encounter a different interface when trying to reach the same control from the keyboard.

I led the WCAG 2.1 audit and front-end remediation. Some repairs concerned the information a control exposed: missing labels and ARIA attributes. Others required changes to how focus moved through the interface. Giving a control a name did not make it reachable, and making it reachable did not settle what its keyboard behaviour should be.

That work also addressed a commercial risk. Institutional contracts associated with $9.2M in annual recurring revenue depended on the product demonstrating the required accessibility compliance. The remediation helped reduce the risk to those existing contracts.

![Keyboard navigation for the main menu](/images/photoshelter-keyboard-navigation.gif)

*Keyboard navigation for PhotoShelter’s main menu.*

The interface used Polymer and Web Components, with interactive elements inside Shadow DOM boundaries. Those boundaries organised the implementation, but keyboard users still needed to move through a menu as a continuous interaction. Focus and keyboard events did not move cleanly between the components.

![The main menu goes from mouse to keyboard control](/images/photoshelter-empty-trash.gif)

*Moving from mouse to keyboard control without a mode switch.*

I built a custom keyboard layer to bridge them. It kept menu items reachable as people moved between components and supported switching between mouse and keyboard without a separate mode. This was behaviour I had to implement across the interface; changing individual controls’ markup would not resolve the navigation problem on its own.

### Carrying the patterns into later changes

The audit identified repairs in the existing product. New development also needed to use the resulting patterns. I established component conventions and review checklists that the team could apply to later work, and mentored four developers on accessibility practices.

I also wrote and maintained Mocha tests used in Jenkins CI/CD pipelines. Those tests supported iterative changes to the production application. Together with the component conventions, they gave the team an established process for changing existing code instead of treating each repair as an isolated implementation.

### A workflow prototype that informed Smart Galleries

Alongside the production work, I collaborated with the Chief Architect and UX team on exploratory workflow prototypes. I built a React-based automation prototype so we could try the proposed behaviour and expose integration problems before committing to the production implementation.

That prototype informed [Smart Galleries](https://support.photoshelterbrands.com/hc/en-us/articles/10657698741655-Smart-Galleries). An internal estimate put the reduction in later implementation effort at roughly 30%. The estimate concerned the later implementation effort; my work was on the exploratory prototype that informed it.

### Testing image analysis in the browser

I also built an OpenCV.js prototype to compare image blur without sending the analysis to a backend. It let me test a lightweight image-analysis workflow in a static-file environment, where the browser had to do the processing.

The blur experiment remained a prototype and did not ship as a standalone feature.

### MSNBC Video: Browsing Around Continuous Playback
*Interaction prototypes and production AngularJS development*
Year: 2014
Tags: Interaction Prototyping, Interaction Design, Front-End Development, AngularJS, Drupal, Media Products
Summary: Proposed and prototyped browsing around continuous video playback, then helped deliver the responsive AngularJS interface and CMS components with MSNBC’s internal team and external vendors.
As Senior Design Technologist and Front-End Developer, I proposed and prototyped the browsing behaviour for MSNBC’s dedicated video experience, then helped deliver the AngularJS interface with the internal team and external vendors.

### A dedicated video experience after the site rebuild

MSNBC needed viewers to be able to look for another story while continuing to watch live or archived coverage. Leaving the viewing page to browse would interrupt that activity. During a live broadcast, the programme could move on while someone was deciding what to watch next.

The dedicated video experience followed the broader MSNBC.com rebuild described in [Lullabot’s account](https://www.lullabot.com/articles/msnbc-video-and-drupalcon-case-study). I worked on the video interface and components for the in-house CMS. The full site redesign was a separate team effort.

Working prototypes before production

I worked with MSNBC’s internal team, external vendors, and stakeholders, first proposing interactions in functional prototypes and then helping implement the agreed behaviour. We had a hard six-month launch deadline, so the prototypes needed to settle questions that would otherwise carry into production development.

I used the prototypes to make the behaviour visible. A static layout could show a player beside a discussion panel. A working version let the team see what happened to the player’s width when that panel opened, and whether browsing still worked while a video was running. We went through several iterations before carrying the agreed interactions into the production AngularJS interface.

Collapsible panels around a running player

My proposal gave the content around the player its own collapsible panels. A viewer could open the discussion, scan the latest coverage, or close the surrounding panels to watch at full width. The player continued running while those browsing choices changed.

Comments sat beside the video and could be dismissed. An “Up next” row below the player placed the next viewing choice near the current clip, while the adjacent video list offered a broader route through the coverage. These controls supported different amounts of browsing without requiring the viewer to leave the page.

Adapting the browsing layout to the screen

The panels also had to work within responsive layouts. A desktop could accommodate horizontal video rows beside a large player. At narrower widths, recommendations moved into vertical lists while the video remained prominent.

I worked through those arrangements in the prototypes and helped carry them into the production interface. The desktop arrangement could not simply shrink to fit. The surrounding recommendations needed a different layout while the player retained its place as the main activity.

![MSNBC video interface with a large player, clip details and an Up next row on the left, and a list of latest videos on the right.](/images/msnbc-interface.png)

*Surviving interface capture from December 2016, rather than launch day. The player, next-video choices, and broader browsing list share the same viewing surface.*

![MSNBC video mockup showing phone, tablet and desktop layouts: the player remains prominent, recommendations stack at narrower widths, and a discussion panel sits beside the desktop player.](/images/msnbc-watch-full-mockup.webp)

*Responsive interface mockup showing the player and surrounding content at different screen widths.*

Through production to launch

My implementation work included AngularJS components for the in-house CMS, integrated with its Drupal backend. I stayed involved as the interaction proposals became production code, working within the responsibilities shared by the internal team and vendors.

The video platform launched within the six-month window. A delayed launch carried a risk of partner litigation; delivering on schedule helped avoid that risk. My contribution extended from proposing the interaction through prototyping and front-end implementation on the team that delivered it.

### WorkBay
*Keep coding tasks and review history available across AI sessions*
Year: 2026
Tags: Developer Tooling, AI-Assisted Development, MCP, Python, SQLite, Review Workflows
Summary: Built WorkBay to preserve task decisions, review findings, and test evidence across AI coding sessions, with SQLite records, MCP retrieval, and checks on the normal Git development path.
I built WorkBay to keep task decisions, review findings, and test evidence available across AI coding sessions. I use it in my own development practice; its public source documents the task database and checks on the normal Git development path.

I move coding work between AI tools and sessions. While developing projects such as [AltContext](/projects/altcontext/), I found that a recap could describe a task as nearly finished while leaving out the review finding that still blocked it. The next session needed the finding and its evidence, not just an account of progress.

I built WorkBay to keep that record outside the conversation. It stores the active task and the decisions made against it, along with review findings and test evidence. A later session can retrieve what remains unresolved, including when I change coding tools.

![Plan, task, work, review, gate, and merge share one durable record. Sessions can end between stages; review findings persist into the gate.](/images/projects/workbay-journey.svg)

*The task record carries decisions, findings, and evidence through the development workflow.*

### Keep a record the next session can use

Each repository has a SQLite database at `.task-state/handoff.db`. A task identifies the work, its branch, and its working copy. Decisions preserve their rationale. Review findings retain their severity and resolution status, while test records keep commands and results.

A session loads a selected context packet from that database. The packet gives it relevant recorded history without requiring the entire earlier conversation. Optional semantic retrieval can find an older decision when the new question uses different wording.

I keep retrieval separate from approval. Finding a similar earlier fix can help a session decide what to inspect, but it cannot close a review finding or authorise a merge. The retrieved record has to be considered against the code being changed now.

### Resume in another coding tool

WorkBay exposes the database through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools. Supported clients include Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and VS Code Copilot. They can read the same project record even though they do not share a conversation.

This makes a change of tool less dependent on access to the previous tool’s transcript. It also helps after a long session has compressed its context: WorkBay can reload the recorded state from the database.

The continuity is limited to what was recorded. Authentication, available tools, and model capabilities still differ between clients, and unrecorded reasoning does not reappear. The useful property is that changing a coding tool does not mean abandoning the project’s accumulated task and review history.

### Carry a review finding through to a change

An authoring agent can submit work to a reviewing agent without passing over its conversation. The reviewer writes findings against the task. When the author resumes, those findings are available to address rather than buried in a separate review transcript.

A finding carries commit references for the fix on the branch and its later merge. That lets another reviewer inspect the code history behind a reported resolution. The review gate checks for unresolved high- and medium-severity findings, including whether a finding has been explicitly deferred or otherwise given an allowed disposition.

I also moved routine task operations into commands that can run without a model turn. Creating a working copy, checking merge readiness, and closing a task do not need an agent to improvise the bookkeeping. Git hooks check the normal development path while they are installed and configured. An unrestricted shell can disable or bypass them; they are not a security boundary.

For self-contained work, WorkBay can hand a bounded task to another backend under a token cap. That worker does not merge its own changes. Review and merge authority remain outside the worker, so producing a change and accepting it are separate steps.

Review the interface as well as the code

A code review may miss a problem that only becomes apparent when the interface is considered as a sequence of screens and states. I use WorkBay’s UX-map workflow to inventory an existing interface or examine a proposed change. The inventory describes screen regions, the states they can show, and the actions and flows between them.

It can be rendered as ASCII screens, Mermaid flow diagrams, and Markdown. People and AI tools can inspect these representations against [Heuristics Canon](/research/heuristics-canon/). Findings can then be attached to the task, addressed in implementation, and checked again after the change.

![An inventory of jobs, screens, states, and flows feeds a renderer. It produces ASCII wireframes, Mermaid flows, and Markdown tables for critique by canon rule ID.](/images/projects/workbay-uxmap.svg)

*The UX-map workflow makes the inventory and review material inspectable before implementation.*

Validation checks whether the map has an acceptable structure. Rendering makes it readable, while critique considers the decisions represented in it. A limited automated check pack can catch an action pointing to a nonexistent screen. None of those operations implements the proposed repair or establishes that the interface will work for its users.

The public WorkBay repository contains the workflow instructions. The renderer and critique implementation belong to a companion Design Canvas package outside the public mirror. The [VSW interaction reference](/research/visual-search-workbench-screen-reference/) shows how text drawings can accompany a product explanation.

### Use and evaluation

I use WorkBay in my own development practice. Wider adoption and quantified effort savings have not been established. The useful evidence available so far concerns persistence, retrieval, and checks against the recorded state.

[Project Memory Outside the Conversation](/research/agent-memory/) explains the mechanism. [Five Questions I Ask the Project Record](/research/interrogating-agent-memory/) follows its use, and [Testing Whether Project Memory Saves Work](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/) sets out the proposed evaluation. Installation instructions and current package details are in the [WorkBay repository](https://github.com/darce/workbay).

### Apple: iPhone X Launch & Marketing Tooling
*Responsive front-end implementation and campaign automation*
Year: 2017
Tags: Front-End Development, Responsive Layout, CSS Animation, JavaScript, Node.js, Bash, Gulp, Campaign Tooling
Summary: Implemented responsive iPhone X launch pages from supplied designs, developed a CSS-animated email campaign, and automated campaign build, preview, and deployment steps.
I implemented responsive iPhone X launch pages with Apple’s marketing and design teams, and built tools to automate email campaign preparation, preview, and deployment.

### iPhone X launch pages

I worked with Apple’s marketing and design teams to turn static iPhone X launch specifications into responsive landing pages. The designs established the visual treatment; I implemented that treatment in the browser under the launch deadlines.

I had to preserve the intended composition as the available width changed. The supplied layouts established the visual target; responsive code had to account for the sizes between them as well. My part of the launch was that implementation, working from the design team’s specifications.

### CSS-animated email campaign

I also prototyped and developed a CSS-animated direct email campaign. The email itself carried the motion, without JavaScript. That introduced a different implementation constraint from the web pages: email clients varied in the CSS they supported.

I used the prototype to work through the motion before developing the campaign implementation. Email-client compatibility was part of that work: an animation that worked on a web page still had to be considered within the more restricted environment of an email.

### Campaign tooling

Preparing campaigns involved repeated build, preview, and deployment steps. I wrote command-line tools in Node.js, Bash, and Gulp to automate that preparation and give the team a repeatable production process.

The automation replaced repeated manual preparation with defined commands. It gave the team a way to prepare another campaign through the same build and preview process, with deployment steps included in the tooling.

### Texting Syria: An Exhibition Across Photographs and Phones
*PHP and Twilio development for Liam Maloney’s installation*
Year: 2014
Tags: Exhibition, Interaction Development, PHP, Twilio, SMS, Documentary Photography
Summary: Built the PHP and Twilio application for Liam Maloney’s Texting Syria installation, delivering previously recorded messages to exhibition visitors’ phones.
I developed the PHP and Twilio application for Texting Syria. Liam Maloney supplied the photographs, text, and translations; I built the software that delivered the exhibition’s messages.

### Bringing the conversations into the exhibition

Liam Maloney photographed Syrians who had fled to Lebanon and were using their phones to keep in touch with family in Homs. His installation paired those photographs with text messages received at the time they were taken. The [Moving Walls collection](https://www.movingwalls.org/moving-walls/23/texting-syria.html) includes the photographs and exchanges translated from Arabic.

The messages gave visitors words that the photographs could not show on their own. To bring those exchanges into the exhibition, I built an application that sent them to visitors’ phones through an SMS service.

### Building the SMS application

I wrote the application in PHP and integrated the Twilio API for message delivery. A visitor connected to the exhibition’s SMS service and received a sequence of texts drawn from the documented exchanges.

These were previously collected messages. Receiving them did not open a live conversation with the people in the photographs. Liam supplied the content and translations, and my work covered the software that made the SMS experience function.

### The visitor’s phone as part of the installation

The visitor read the texts in their own message inbox, where they would ordinarily receive messages from people they knew. That familiar interface became part of the installation alongside the photographs on display.

The application connected the exhibition material to that everyday act of receiving a message. It used the phone already in the visitor’s hand as the place where the written exchange appeared.

Texting Syria’s [Photoville New York exhibition record](https://photoville.com/projects/texting-syria/) credits Liam Maloney, with coding by Daniel Arce. The [Moving Walls 23 artist statement](https://www.movingwalls.org/moving-walls/23/texting-syria.html) describes Liam’s documentary intent and the larger body of work to which the installation belongs.

### barbarabeirne.com: Archive Recovery & Web Components Rebuild
*Recovering the photographs and rebuilding their web presentation*
Year: 2026
Tags: Web Components, JavaScript, Sass, Rollup, Accessibility, Archive Recovery
Summary: Recovered the images embedded in Barbara Beirne’s defunct Flash site, then rebuilt its web presentation with Web Components, keyboard navigation, and a full-screen carousel.
I recovered the photographs from Barbara Beirne’s non-functional Flash site and rebuilt her portfolio around them. A later Web Components rebuild added keyboard navigation and a full-screen carousel.

### Recovering a Flash archive

Barbara Beirne’s photography archive was held inside a Flash website that had stopped working years earlier. The original source files were unavailable, and the original developer could not be brought back into the project. Before I could rebuild the portfolio, I needed to recover the photographs from the published site.

The surviving file was a compiled `.SWF`. It contained the images, but it was not an editable source project or a folder of photographs ready to move into a new website. That made asset recovery the first part of the development work.

### Recovering the images

I used [FFDec](https://blog.free-decompiler.com/), an open-source Flash decompiler, to extract the images embedded in the binary. Getting clean exports took additional work, but I recovered the full embedded image set and used it for the initial rebuild.

![Black and white image of three Cambodian teens standing in front of high school lockers](/images/barbara-beirne-extracted-image.png)

*Image extracted from the compiled Flash file using FFDec.*

Recovering those assets gave the project usable photographs again. It also let the new site present the work without depending on the Flash application that had previously contained it.

### Rebuilding with Web Components

Once the archive was recovered and the initial site rebuilt, I returned to its web presentation. I rewrote the site with Web Components and JavaScript, using Rollup for the build and Sass for styling.

I implemented keyboard interaction for the navigation and full-screen carousel. Visitors could use those parts of the interface without relying on a mouse.

### Presenting her images

We chose a minimal, stark design to give Barbara’s photographs room. The navigation and viewing controls had to support looking through the archive without dominating the page.

The full-screen carousel provides a larger view of a photograph, while the navigation supports moving through the archive. That made room for sustained viewing as well as moving on to the next photograph.

![A group of children climbing on a large pile of debris, one waving the Ulster Banner. Image by Barbara Beirne](/images/barbara-beirne-custom-carousel-belfast-8.jpg)

### Feedback on the recovery

Alison Cornyn, an artist and the co-founder and creative director of Picture Projects, wrote after the recovery and initial rebuild:

> “Daniel came up with suggestions and solutions that were beyond what the original site had and brought it all to life.”

*Alison Cornyn.*

### bauhausdances.org: Visual Identity & Custom WordPress Theme
*Visual design drawn from the films, implemented in WordPress*
Year: 2023
Tags: Visual Design, WordPress, Custom Theme, PHP, CSS Animation, JavaScript, Self-Hosted Video
Summary: Designed a film-derived visual treatment and built a custom WordPress theme for Debra McCall’s Bauhaus Dances, with self-hosted video and caching.
Debra McCall supplied the films of her 1982 reconstruction of Oskar Schlemmer’s Bauhaus Dances. I designed and built their web presentation, including the visual treatment and a custom WordPress theme.

### A visual treatment drawn from the films

Debra McCall wanted a new website for the films of her 1982 reconstruction of Oskar Schlemmer’s Bauhaus Dances. She supplied the films. My work was to develop their web presentation and build a site she could manage independently.

The visual direction came from the Hoop Dance sequence. White rings form changing geometric arrangements around the dancer against a dark stage. I used those rings as the basis for the site’s visual treatment and interaction language, connecting the surrounding design to a specific passage in the films.

![Hoop Dance performance. A dancer stands on one foot with her left foot stretched back, holding five white rings. Two rings form concentric circles near her head, three form concentric circles below her hips.](/images/bauhaus-dances-hoop-dance.jpg)

A subtle ring-based interaction carries that idea into the interface. The motion refers back to the filmed performance while leaving the films as the main material to watch. The same film sequence therefore informed both the graphic treatment and the motion I implemented.

A custom WordPress theme for the films

I built the site as a custom WordPress theme using [Underscores](https://underscores.me/) as the starting point. The theme combined PHP with JavaScript and CSS animation. WordPress provided the content-management interface, while the custom theme let me implement the film-derived design.

That separation mattered for the handover. The visual treatment could be specific to this project without requiring the client to return to the code for routine content management. The client could manage the content through WordPress while the theme controlled its presentation.

### Self-hosted video

I implemented self-hosted video so the presentation did not depend on third-party embeds. I also added caching to support delivery of the media-heavy site.

The result was a WordPress site built around McCall’s supplied films, with their presentation and supporting content under the site’s own management.

## Research

### Finding a Visual Direction with UMAP
*How similarity search becomes a way to explore a photo collection*
Tags: Visual Search, UMAP, Interaction Design, On-Device ML, Research
Summary: How Visual Search Workbench connects search, a UMAP map, and an image grid to help people explore a photo collection and develop a visual direction.
A design study of the implemented interaction: how a search, a UMAP map, and an image grid support visual exploration.

A useful picture can change what you are looking for. You may start with a subject in mind, then notice a colour relationship or composition worth following. That shift interests me because it turns search into part of developing an idea.

[Visual Search Workbench](/projects/visual-search-workbench/) gives that shift a path through a photo collection. A search produces candidates; a candidate can become the next query. Alongside the search, a UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) map offers regions of related images to explore.

A selected map region opens its photographs in the linked image grid, where their composition, colour, and subject can be judged together.

Chosen photo folders supply an index. Words or a reference image query that index to produce candidate photographs.

_Search is a path into the collection; the candidates still need visual judgment._

![The Similarity map in Visual Search Workbench, with photographs from a selected region available in the grid.](/images/work/sis-layers-umap.png)

*Application capture from version 0.2.0. The companion interaction reference draws on the 0.2.3 product record.*

## Search can lead somewhere you did not expect

Search often starts with a fairly definite task: find a photograph you remember. A description can bring likely candidates into view even when you have forgotten the filename. Once you recognise the picture, the search has done its job.

Visual exploration has a less definite endpoint. A photograph can be useful because it suggests what to look for next. In a reference collection, for example, you might follow a visual resemblance toward a composition you had not yet formulated. The value of that next image depends on the idea you are developing, not only on its match to the original words.

VSW lets a result become the next query through **Find similar**. The chosen image becomes the reference for a new ranking, with its name visible above the results. **Back to text results** provides a return to the earlier search. These controls make it possible to follow an image without treating every query as an unrelated start.

Text results contain photograph B. Open B, choose Find similar to use it as a reference, then return with Back to text results.

_A chosen photograph changes the query; the return path recovers the earlier text results._

![A photograph used as a Find similar reference, with the reference named and a return to text results available.](/images/work/sis-similarity-search.png)

## The map makes related images browsable

A ranked list arranges candidates around one query. A map provides a different way to look through the material: inspect a region, see which pictures it contains, and choose where to go next. UMAP supplies the arrangement for VSW’s Similarity view.

### How UMAP works, in plain terms

The app’s image model turns each photograph into an **embedding**, a list of numbers used to compare images. Those numbers work together as a representation; individual entries are not labels such as “red,” “flower,” or “portrait.” Comparing the representations gives the software a way to find nearby images without consulting manually assigned tags.

Those nearby images form **neighbourhoods**. UMAP represents neighbourhood relationships as a weighted graph: a network of connections whose strengths reflect the local relationships in the input. It then looks for a lower-dimensional arrangement that preserves those relationships as well as possible. This is the graph-and-layout process described in the [UMAP authors’ explanation](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/how_umap_works.html).

The arrangement becomes the map on screen. Its purpose is to make some of those relationships available to explore while accepting that a compact layout loses information. The image model supplies the representations; UMAP arranges them; the person decides which pictures are worth following.

### What the arrangement means

A neighbourhood is a place to investigate, not a category the app has established. Its pictures may be useful together, or their resemblance may be unimportant to the current brief. The photographs themselves let you make that distinction.

The layout also changes how relationships look. A wide gap between groups is not an exact measure of their difference, and a dense patch does not establish the density of the original representations. Apparent splits can arise during the reduction, as the [UMAP clustering guide](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/clustering.html) explains.

Two settings help explain why maps can look different: **neighbourhood size** and **minimum distance**. Neighbourhood size determines how broadly the method looks around each item, shifting emphasis between fine local detail and a wider arrangement. Minimum distance affects how tightly points can pack in the layout. The [parameter guide](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/parameters.html) illustrates both effects. These are explanations of the method, not controls I am claiming the current app exposes.

## The image grid makes the map usable

A region on the map becomes an image selection. That selection appears in the grid, where you can inspect the photographs at a useful size. A promising photograph can then supply the reference for another search.

```text
Similarity overview
┌───────────────────────────┐
│   . .              . .    │
│  ┌─────────┐              │
│  │ A  B  C │      . .     │
│  └─────────┘              │
│       . .                 │
└───────────────────────────┘
       Selected region
              │
              ▾
      Linked image grid
      ┌───────────────────┐
      │ [A]  [B]  [C]     │
      │ Inspect these     │
      │ photographs       │
      └───────────────────┘
```

_Conceptual map-to-grid relationship, not a reconstruction of the application: selecting a region containing photographs A, B, and C shows those same photographs in the linked grid. Other regions remain outside the selection._

The grid and map also need distinct interpretations. A search ranking compares the query with the image representations. The distance between marks on the displayed map is not that ranking. Keeping those roles clear lets the map support browsing without asking it to be a precise measuring instrument.

## Keep the exploration on an everyday Mac

Local processing was a design constraint for the app. The photographs stay in the folders the person chooses, and the models ship with the application. I tested that arrangement on an 8 GB Apple Silicon Mac.

That constraint extends beyond running the model. My [case study](/projects/visual-search-workbench/#look-at-the-selection-by-place-or-time) describes the latest-range decision, slider corrections, and metadata filling in after the plot and timeline appear. I associate those changes with the [0.2.6 release record](https://github.com/darce/visual-search-workbench/releases/tag/v0.2.6), which was unavailable during this article’s source review; the release-specific claims remain my account. The 8 GB test identifies a working configuration; larger-library performance and peak memory still need measurement.

## Test retrieval and exploration separately

The design now has an implementation to evaluate. I review the path from query to selection to next action using screen inventories and the running app. The [interaction reference](/research/visual-search-workbench-screen-reference/) makes that path inspectable. WorkBay and the [Heuristics Canon](/research/heuristics-canon/) support my reviews; no external user study has run.

That evaluation needs to distinguish **retrieval** from **exploration**. Retrieval asks whether someone can find a remembered photograph. Exploration asks whether someone can assemble useful references for a creative brief, including pictures that change the direction of the brief.

For retrieval, I would examine completion, mistakes, and effort. For exploration, I would examine the images people keep, the paths they take, and their reasons for continuing from one picture to another. Comparing the map with the grid and image-to-image search would help establish what the map contributes.

An exploration study would need to allow for a useful selection that takes someone beyond the subject they first searched for.

### Visual Search Workbench: Search and Exploration
*Follow a query into similar images, a map selection, and further exploration*
Tags: Visual Search, UMAP, Interaction Design, Interface Reference
Summary: An interaction reference for Visual Search Workbench: begin with words or a picture, follow similar images, and inspect a UMAP map selection in the image grid.
This selective interaction reference combines existing application captures with clearly labelled explanatory schematics.

This reference follows a path through [Visual Search Workbench](/projects/visual-search-workbench/): give the search a starting point, make a promising picture the next query, then explore related material on the Similarity map. The selected images remain available in the grid for inspection and further use.

The current downloadable release is 0.2.6. The application captures remain the existing 0.2.0 screenshots; the descriptions draw on the 0.2.3 product record. **The workflow graphics are explanatory schematics, not screenshots, exact layouts, or newly verified interface strings.** Letters stand for photographs rather than measured search results.

## 1. Give the search a starting point

Search choices: words and a reference image are alternative query inputs. Both lead to candidate photographs in the image grid.

_Schematic: two ways to start a search._

The search uses an index of the folders you choose. The index lets the app compare their photographs while the originals remain in place. It accepts a text query or a reference image, with neither route requiring advance tagging.

A text query is useful when you can describe what you want. A reference image is useful when showing an example is easier. Both routes lead to candidates that you can inspect in the image grid.

## 2. Make a result the next query

A selected photograph opens for inspection. **Find similar** makes that photograph the reference for another search.

The new view names the reference and offers **Back to text results**, keeping the change of query visible.

Screen storyboard: open photograph B from text results. Find similar makes B the reference for new results E, F, and G. Back to text results returns to the original results.

_Schematic: B is the new query._

![Find similar results with a flower photograph identified as the reference image.](/images/work/sis-similarity-search.png)

## 3. Explore a region on the Similarity map

![The Similarity view and the photographs associated with a selected region.](/images/work/sis-layers-umap.png)

The **Similarity** view offers a spatial arrangement of related images. That arrangement is built with UMAP, which takes numerical image representations, identifies their neighbourhood relationships, and looks for a layout that preserves those relationships in fewer dimensions.

In practical terms, UMAP turns many-number comparisons into places to browse on a screen. Those places are suggestions for exploration, not automatically named categories. The [design article](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/) explains the method and how it differs from search ranking.

Linked views: selecting a map region containing A, B, and C shows the same photographs in the image grid. The outlined region and outlined grid items identify the same selection; other map points remain outside it.

_Schematic: A, B and C stay selected in both views._

A selected region becomes a set of photographs in the linked grid. The grid lets you inspect the images behind the marks and choose whether any is worth following.

Spacing between map marks is not an exact measure of how different the photographs are. Inspect the selection in the grid to judge the images themselves.

## 4. Examine the selection by place or time

The selected material can be examined through **Similarity**, **Places**, and **Timeline**. Each view organises the collection using different information.

| View | Basis of the view |
| --- | --- |
| Similarity | Relationships between numerical image representations. |
| Places | Recorded coordinates, explored geographically. |
| Timeline | Dates, explored across broader or narrower periods. |

Selection carries between the views, and each view retains its zoom and pan when you change tabs. The views therefore offer different routes through related material without requiring you to rebuild the view each time.

A place-based selection can also include photographs outside the current text results. Those photographs are listed without a search rank, keeping the geographic selection distinct from the query’s ranking.

## 5. Inspect a photograph or use a cutout

![A cat image with experimental cutout layers available for inspection.](/images/work/sis-cat-layers-detail.png)

An individual photograph can be inspected with its available file metadata. It can also supply a subject for the experimental cutout workflow, which proposes layers with transparent backgrounds.

The proposed layers can be inspected and saved for use elsewhere. A recognisable subject does not guarantee a usable separation or edge, so the cutout still needs checking. This remains a secondary workflow alongside search and exploration.

## Use the reference to review the interaction

I use this reference to check whether each selection has a clear next action and a way to return to the earlier search.

The diagrams separate query choices, screen changes, and selection links. They are selective explanations; the running interface still needs to be checked for behaviour and visual quality. Text wireframes remain useful for describing the arrangement of interface elements.

Read [Finding a Visual Direction with UMAP](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/) for the design idea, or return to the [product page](/projects/visual-search-workbench/) for installation and release status.

### Project Memory Outside the Conversation
*The record, retrieval layer, and context packet behind WorkBay*
Tags: Agent Workflows, SQLite, Semantic Retrieval, Research
Summary: WorkBay separates the stored project record from the retrieval layer that finds it and the context packet a coding session reads.
SQLite preserves decisions and evidence; exact lookup, text search, and optional semantic retrieval supply selected records to the next coding session.

A later coding session needs more than an account of what happened. It may need the reason an approach was rejected, the finding that remains unresolved, or the test result behind a completion claim. [WorkBay](/projects/workbay/) keeps that material in a project record outside the conversation.

The design has three parts: a **record**, a **retrieval layer**, and a **context packet**. The record preserves decisions and evidence. The retrieval layer finds material that may matter to the current task. The context packet gives the next session a selected portion to read.

![Session A writes decisions, findings, and results into handoff.db. Its conversation is outside session B’s view, but selected records reach session B as a small context packet.](/images/research/memory-loop.svg?v=2)

*The database connects sessions: the next conversation receives a selection of recorded work without needing the earlier transcript.*

I use this record to [examine earlier decisions](/research/interrogating-agent-memory/). Whether supplying it reduces work at comparable quality remains a [question for evaluation](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/).

## The record preserves decisions and evidence

In my WorkBay setup, each repository has a SQLite file at `.task-state/handoff.db`. SQLite stores the database locally without requiring a separate database server. The database contains tasks, decisions, review findings, blockers, and test records. The [project’s persistence description](https://github.com/darce/workbay#what-persists-exactly) supports this broad architecture; this article describes my setup, rather than a guarantee about every installation.

Those records keep different aspects of the work distinct. A decision has a rationale. A finding has a status and a recorded resolution. A test has a command and result, with task and commit information helping connect the evidence to the work it concerns.

A later session can therefore retrieve a decision as a decision. It need not reconstruct the rationale from a recap saying that planning was completed. The rationale still needs to be checked against present requirements, but the earlier reasoning is available for that check.

## The retrieval layer finds material in the record

Retrieval depends on what the session already knows. A known task or finding can be looked up directly. Known wording can be found through full-text search. A question phrased differently from the earlier record can use optional semantic retrieval.

Semantic retrieval compares numerical representations called **embeddings**. An embedding represents a piece of text as a list of numbers. Comparing these representations can bring related records into view even when their wording differs. Reimers and Gurevych’s [Sentence-BERT paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084) demonstrates this approach for sentence similarity; it does not identify the model or establish retrieval quality in my WorkBay setup.

![A question becomes a numerical vector. In a schematic two-dimensional view, it sits near an earlier rationale and farther from an unrelated note.](/images/research/memory-vector.svg?v=2)

*The nearby rationale is a candidate to read. This simplified view shows similarity, which does not establish that the earlier constraint still applies.*

Suppose retrieval finds the rationale for an approach rejected earlier. The session can compare the recorded constraint with the current implementation before deciding whether that rejection still holds.

### Keep the index tied to the record

The embeddings form an index over selected fields in the database. The design links each index entry to its source record and a text fingerprint: a value computed from the text to detect when it changes. Those records remain available independently of the index, so the index can be rebuilt without becoming the authoritative version of a decision.

The related-prior-work tool is intended to return candidates for a human or agent to read. My design rule is that a candidate must never, by itself, close a finding or authorise a merge. Similarity can change which record looks worth inspecting; it cannot establish that two findings are duplicates or that either has been fixed.

A lookup needs to distinguish an empty store from an unavailable embedding service, an incompatible index, or no candidate meeting the similarity cutoff. An empty result alone cannot prove the relevant history is absent. These are safeguards to check in the installed version. The exact [retrieval module](https://github.com/darce/workbay/blob/main/packages/mcp-workbay-handoff/src/workbay_handoff_mcp/embeddings/related_prior_work.py) was unavailable during this article’s source review, so its current status categories and enforcement are not verified here.

## The context packet gives the session a selection

A context packet brings selected records into the current conversation. The packet must be bounded because the conversation still has finite space. Loading every past record would compete with the task the session is meant to complete.

![The stored record feeds two alternative retrieval paths: exact lookup and full-text search, or optional semantic search. Both lead to a selected context packet; the semantic index links back to its source rows.](/images/research/memory-layers.svg?v=2)

*Read from the top down: preserve the record, choose a retrieval path, then select what the session needs. Semantic search is optional.*

The choice of records therefore matters. In an earlier audit of my repositories, review findings accounted for roughly four fifths of embedded entries, with decision rationales making up most of the remainder. This is my unverified audit summary: no dated extract, row counts, or per-project denominator accompanies it. It describes the material I reported having available, rather than a current distribution or a target for other projects.

A selected record earns its place in the packet if it supplies a constraint, unresolved finding, or other evidence the next decision needs. A paragraph that merely sounds relevant can consume the same space without helping the task.

## Portability follows the record

The structured record can be exported and read by different supported coding tools. A session in a new tool can retrieve history written by another tool without having its entire conversation. The new tool still needs its own authentication and setup, and its capabilities may differ.

The database stays out of version control by default because it can contain sensitive project material. Keeping the file local does not make every use of its contents private: a context packet sent to a hosted model sends that selected material to the provider. Export and model use both require attention to what the record contains.

![A local database stays out of version control by default. Selected rows can cross the machine boundary through an export or a packet sent to a hosted model.](/images/research/memory-boundary.svg?v=2)

*Local storage and model use have different boundaries. Sending a context packet to a hosted model sends those selected records to its provider.*

## Test what the record changes

Reasoning that was never recorded cannot be retrieved, and useful records can still be missed. The [proposed evaluation](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/) tests the resulting question: does a session receiving selected history complete comparable work with less effort?

### Five Questions I Ask the Project Record
*Look for recurring trouble, earlier fixes, decision reasons, completion evidence, and failed approaches*
Tags: Agent Workflows, Project Memory, Field Notes
Summary: Five recurring questions show how I use WorkBay’s project record to examine an earlier decision before making the next one.
These are field observations from my development practice, not a controlled productivity study.

I use the project record when the next coding decision depends on work outside the current conversation. The record can bring back an earlier rationale or show that a new-looking failure has already occurred across several tasks.

In [WorkBay](/projects/workbay/), I look up decisions, findings, test records, or blockers according to what the current task needs.

[Project Memory Outside the Conversation](/research/agent-memory/) explains how those records are stored and retrieved.

## Where does trouble repeat?

A review usually concerns the work in front of it. A sequence of reviews can reveal trouble that keeps returning across tasks. The project record makes that sequence available even when no single session has seen all of it.

![A column of records marks failed reviews in coral. One session sees only two rows, while a cluster of failures appears farther down the complete record.](/images/research/memory-window.svg?v=2)

*A session sees a small slice; the record can reveal repetition across tasks. The rows are schematic, not the audit sample.*

In my summary of an earlier audit, roughly three quarters of the recorded reviews in a small project had failed. The audit date, review count, and underlying rows are not available here; this remains an author-reported observation. That pattern prompted a closer look at the architecture. The count did not establish the cause: task selection and review practice could also have affected the proportion.

I inspected the findings behind the count to see whether they shared a constraint or arose from different causes. The proportion directed that investigation; the findings had to support the diagnosis.

## Does a useful fix already exist?

A new finding may resemble a problem recorded under different wording. Semantic retrieval—searching by similarity between numerical text representations—can surface an earlier resolution, which a human or agent can compare with the current code.

The resolution may contain more than a patch. It can preserve the constraint that made the patch necessary or the reason a simpler change failed. That explanation helps determine whether the earlier fix applies now.

An earlier fix remains a candidate until its conditions and recorded status have been checked. Copying the patch without that check would replace repeated investigation with a different risk: applying the right answer to the wrong problem.

## Why was this approach chosen?

A decision record preserves the reasons behind a choice. Those reasons give a later discussion a starting point even when the people or tools involved were absent from the original conversation.

For example, a later session may question why a site uses static output rather than server rendering. The recorded rationale can identify the requirements the choice addressed. Those requirements can then be compared with the needs of the current work.

A changed requirement may justify a changed decision. The record should make that change deliberate, not keep the original choice closed forever. Its value is distinguishing a new reason from an old debate whose reasoning has been forgotten.

## What supports the completion claim?

A completion claim needs evidence tied to the work being assessed. In my WorkBay workflow, review verdicts (the reviewer’s pass or fail decision) and test records sit alongside task and commit information. A commit identifies a particular revision of the code. That information lets another reviewer inspect which commands ran, what they returned, and which revision they concern.

The revision matters because a test result from earlier code does not automatically establish the state of the current code. A useful review follows the evidence back to the change instead of relying on a summary saying that the task passed.

A second model can be given that evidence without inheriting the author’s conversation. Independence of the conversation does not guarantee a correct review; the reviewer still needs to examine the changed code and the relevant checks. Semantic search may help locate the relevant discussion, but the completion assessment depends on the exact records and the code.

## What has already failed?

A failed approach leaves information that can disappear from a recap of the eventual success. Blockers and abandoned attempts preserve that information, including why the approach was set aside.

The reason distinguishes an option that was temporarily unavailable from one that produced incorrect results. An unavailable dependency may later become usable. An incorrect result may expose a constraint that still applies.

The history therefore does not forbid another attempt. It makes the next attempt answer a specific question: what has changed since this failed?

## From a useful lookup to an evaluated benefit

My use of these lookups has not established how often retrieval finds the right material or how much work it saves.

[Testing Whether Project Memory Saves Work](/research/economics-of-agent-memory/) proposes a comparison of task effort and quality to evaluate that benefit.

### Testing Whether Project Memory Saves Work
*What an audit shows, what a comparison must test, and what would count as a useful result*
Tags: Agent Workflows, Evaluation, Token Use, Research
Summary: An audit snapshot describes WorkBay context packets. A proposed paired comparison tests whether they reduce task token use without lowering quality.
An author-reported audit supplies descriptive figures with incomplete provenance. A proposed paired trial would test a 20% token-reduction target at comparable quality.

Project history is worth supplying to a coding session when it helps the session complete the task. It may prevent a repeated investigation or bring an important constraint back into view. It may also distract the agent or revive a decision that no longer applies.

A task-relevant context packet is useful if it reduces total token use **without lowering outcome quality**. Fewer tokens alone would not establish a useful result if the agent completed less of the task or introduced more errors.

The audit gives a starting point for that test: the recorded size and contents of context packets. It cannot establish their effect on task outcomes.

## The audit snapshot describes cost and contents

My summary of an earlier audit describes three project `handoff.db` databases. The audit date and reproducible extract are unavailable here. A **token** is a unit of text processed by a model; task totals can include many requests and retries. Its summary reported small initial context packets alongside much larger recorded task totals. It also found that most findings marked resolved had a written resolution.

| Audit observation | What it describes |
| --- | --- |
| About 300 tokens in the average compact packet | The recorded size of an initial selection of project history. |
| A median recorded task near three hundred thousand tokens | Task-level totals, rather than the cost of one model request. |
| Recorded tasks ranging from a few thousand to hundreds of millions of tokens | A heterogeneous workload, including very large tasks split across worker lanes. |
| About 99% of resolved findings carrying a written resolution; no audited codebase below 97% | Whether a resolution was recorded, not whether another task would benefit from it. |

These figures are unverified, author-reported aggregates from that audit. The summary does not provide the underlying rows or per-measure sample sizes, so the figures should not be treated as a general performance benchmark.

![On a logarithmic ruler, the average packet is around three hundred tokens and the median recorded task around three hundred thousand, about three tenfold steps apart.](/images/research/econ-scale.svg?v=3)

*Each step is ten times the tokens. The markers compare two audit aggregates; they do not measure savings or the full cost of memory.*

Dividing those two summary figures gives `300 / 300,000 = 0.001`, or 0.1%. This compares a mean packet size with a median task total across different observations; it is neither a matched-task overhead estimate nor a savings measurement. Retrieval, later context use, and decisions made from stale material can add costs beyond that initial packet. These token aggregates do not establish a monetary return.

### The audit cannot establish an effect

The audit’s main limitation is an instrumentation mismatch. Interactive sessions received context packets but lacked the audited task-level token measurement used in the analysis. Orchestrated worker lanes supplied token measurements but did not receive those packets.

![Interactive sessions have packet marks but no audited token meter. Orchestrated lanes have meter marks but no packets. A crossed-out connection shows the missing overlap.](/images/research/econ-gap.svg?v=2)

*In this audit, one group received the intervention and the other supplied the measurement. Neither group supplies both sides needed to estimate the effect.*

That mismatch prevents a meaningful treated-versus-untreated comparison. The two groups differ in their work and measurement as well as their use of project history. A controlled comparison must record both the intervention and its cost for the same assigned tasks.

The resolution figures have a similar boundary. A written resolution establishes that material exists to retrieve. It does not establish that retrieval selects the right resolution, or that an agent uses it well. Those effects belong in the comparison.

## The comparison tests whether the packet changes the work

The proposed comparison runs each selected task twice from the same base commit: once with a frozen, task-relevant packet and once without that packet. Both runs receive the same task specification, model configuration, and resource limits. Their order is randomised, and neither updates shared memory until the pair is complete.

![Four stages: calibrate variation with A/A pairs, compare relevant and unrelated packets, run matched memory-versus-cold pairs, then report token effects alongside blinded quality.](/images/research/econ-design.svg?v=4)

*The proposed sequence separates normal run-to-run variation, the relevance of the content, and the effect of supplying it. The readout must include quality.*

**Calibration** uses A/A pairs: two cold runs with the same starting conditions. The variation between those attempts estimates how much results can differ without the memory intervention. That variation informs the sample-size procedure for the main comparison.

**The content probe** compares a relevant packet with an equally sized unrelated packet. This tests whether relevant content makes a difference beyond merely adding text. A relevant-versus-unrelated result would not, by itself, establish a benefit over receiving no packet.

**Matched task pairs** provide the no-packet comparison. Each pair contains one run with the relevant packet and one without it. A reviewer who does not know which condition produced the work scores both results against a fixed rubric. The system records total tokens per assigned task, including unsuccessful attempts. The protocol must count packet preparation, embedding and retrieval, repeated context input, output, retries, and review effort consistently. For money rather than tokens, each category needs its applicable rate; cached input and output may cost different amounts. This article supplies no provider-price forecast.

Keeping unsuccessful attempts in the analysis matters because a quick failure can use fewer tokens than a completed task. The quality assessment and failure rate must therefore accompany the token result.

## The decision criterion includes quality

The proposal uses a **quality margin**: the largest acceptable deterioration on a predefined review rubric. It sets a target of at least a **20% reduction in token use**, with blinded quality kept within an acceptable margin declared before the trial. This is a proposed decision criterion; no controlled savings result has been measured.

The readout should report the paired effect with an uncertainty interval, alongside the quality comparison and failure rate. A reduction in tokens would qualify only if the quality condition also holds. For each task, compare the memory-run total with the cold-run total before aggregating; report absolute totals as well as ratios, since a small-task percentage can hide a large-task cost. An inconclusive interval would remain inconclusive rather than being presented as a savings result.

The initial comparison would concern one repository’s workload. A result there would not establish the same effect for other projects, models, or teams without further evaluation.

## Specify the measurement before running it
