The protocol still needs its operational definitions completed. The interactive task meter and packet-selection rule must be recorded and frozen. The quality rubric, acceptable quality margin, and sample-size procedure (how many task pairs the uncertainty target requires) must be specified before the main comparison.

Those definitions determine what the result will mean. Changing them after inspecting the results could change which runs count as successful or which apparent saving meets the target. Fixing them first makes the eventual decision checkable.

This is a proposed evaluation, not a completed or externally registered study. Canon v0.25.6 supplies review prompts, not empirical validation: [UXR-01 **Match claim to validation level**](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/v0.25.6/lexicons/interaction-ux.md#uxr-01) (*Visualization Analysis and Design (Munzner)*; *Spatial Semiotics and Spatial Mental Models*, ch. 3) keeps the method aligned with the claim. [EXP-01 **Base-rate idea failure**](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/v0.25.6/lexicons/epistemics.md#exp-01) (*Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments*, ch. 1) asks for a controlled comparison or an explicitly lower-trust method.

## The decision in the meantime

I use WorkBay to retain inspectable project history and resume work across coding sessions. Until the comparison is run, I can assess the recorded history and retrieval behaviour, but cannot claim measured effort savings.

[Project Memory Outside the Conversation](/research/agent-memory/) describes that implementation. [Five Questions I Ask the Project Record](/research/interrogating-agent-memory/) describes how I use it in practice.

### Heuristics Canon
*Connect a review finding to a reason for changing the work*
Tags: Design Review, Engineering, Writing, Research
Summary: Heuristics Canon gives design, engineering, and writing reviews specific triggers and questions, with references that let another reviewer examine the reasoning.
I maintain this collection for human and AI reviews. The rules support critique; they do not replace judgment.

A review becomes useful when its finding is specific enough to examine. “Improve the navigation” leaves the problem open to interpretation. A finding that identifies two conflicting destinations gives the designer something to inspect and a decision to make.

Heuristics Canon is a collection I maintain to support that kind of critique in design, engineering, and writing. I use it with people and AI tools to connect an observed issue to a reason for changing it. A cited rule makes that reason available to challenge as well as to apply.

## Make the rule inspectable

A Canon rule has an observable **trigger**, a proposed **action**, and a **question** that tests whether it applies. The trigger identifies a situation in the artifact under review. The action suggests what to do about it. The question helps the reviewer decide whether the situation actually warrants that response.

A stable ID identifies the rule, and a source reference records its basis. This article uses the pinned release **v0.25.6**. Its three force levels distinguish a blocking rule (**B**), a strong default requiring a named exemption (**S**), and a contextual judgment (**J**). A rule’s trigger and exemptions still decide whether it applies. Those references let another reviewer follow the reasoning without relying on the first reviewer’s explanation alone. Where the basis is provisional or unsourced practice, the collection marks that distinction.

The rules are grouped into lexicons, including interaction design, accessibility, engineering, and writing. These are parts of the same review practice: an interface decision may depend on implementation constraints, while a claim about that interface may need a different kind of evidence. A review retrieves the relevant rules rather than applying the whole collection as a checklist.

## Review a map and the images it represents

Visual Search Workbench connects a Similarity map with an image grid. Reviewing that connection raises two separate questions: **does the selection remain recognisable across the views**, and **does the explanation describe the map accurately**?

**The selection** is a coordination problem. Selecting a region on the map should leave the same material recognisable in the grid, where the photographs can be inspected. The Canon records that principle as [VIZ-15 **Coordinate multiple views**](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/v0.25.6/lexicons/interaction-ux.md#viz-15) (*Visualization Analysis and Design (Munzner)*).

**The explanation** is an interpretation problem. Wording that presents a gap between UMAP groups as an exact measure of visual difference would claim more than the layout supports. [VIZ-18 **A topology-preserving projection is not a metric map**](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/v0.25.6/lexicons/interaction-ux.md#viz-18) (*UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection*) supplies a check on that inference.

These examples show how a rule can focus a critique. They do not establish that the map helps people explore a collection. The [VSW design article](/research/visual-search-workbench-process/) treats that as a separate evaluation question.

## Carry the finding into the work

My workflow combines the Canon with [WorkBay](/projects/workbay/). An interface can be inventoried in a UX map and rendered as text screens or flow diagrams. A reviewer examines those representations and records a finding with the rule and artifact it concerns.

In my workflow, a task stores the finding alongside the change that addresses it. A useful finding names the artifact, the observed defect, the triggered rule’s ID and name, its source and locator, and the version used. For example: a caption treats a UMAP gap as a measured difference; narrow the caption under VIZ-18, then check the revised wording against the method’s limits. On the next review, the reviewer can compare the result with the original issue and record whether it was resolved.

The running interface remains part of that review. A map can expose an action or flow, but it does not reproduce the entire visual and interactive experience.

## Question the finding before changing the product

Before changing the product, I check whether the cited defect actually exists.

In an earlier review from my practice, an agent proposed changing roughly forty code sites it had classified as defective. Checking that classification first found that about a third were false positives, and the proposed sweep narrowed. The review date, inspected-site list, and adjudication record are not supplied here. These are unverified figures from my practice, not an accuracy measurement for the Canon.

Another recorded correction concerned a failure described as present in shipped work. The failure existed only in a constructed test input, so the claim had to be narrowed before it could justify a production change. In both cases, examining the basis of the finding changed the proposed work.

## Keep the source and version with the reasoning

A source reference lets the reviewer examine the basis of a rule. The artifact must still match its trigger, and an exception may make the proposed action inappropriate.

The writing lexicon makes this boundary explicit: some rules are provisional editorial checks, not proof of AI authorship. Repeating a topic can help a reader follow an explanation, for example; repetition alone does not establish that the prose should be changed. The effect on the passage matters.

A review also needs the version of the rule it used. An ID can remain stable while the wording or source changes. I first retrieve only rules whose triggers match the artifact, then read their complete rows, related principles, and every reasoning card listing the kept IDs. Digest checks detect a changed release copy; they do not prove the rules are correct. The [consumer guide](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon/blob/v0.25.6/AGENTS.md) describes version and digest checks so the basis of an earlier critique can be recovered.

## Measure review quality, not the number of citations

Whether the collection improves review outcomes over a smaller checklist or another reviewer remains unmeasured.

A comparison would need to examine consequential findings, missed defects, false positives, and reviewer effort on comparable artifacts. Counting cited rule IDs would measure activity without showing which consequential defects the review found or missed.

The [public repository](https://github.com/darce/heuristics-canon) contains the rules, source references, and longer reasoning cards for decisions that need more context.

### 3D Without Canvas or WebGL
*Rotation matrices and perspective projection in TypeScript and CSS*
Tags: Linear Algebra, 3D Graphics, TypeScript, DOM Manipulation, CSS Transforms
Summary: A browser experiment that makes rotation matrices and perspective projection, normally abstracted by WebGL, visible using only TypeScript, DOM elements, and CSS transforms
Move your mouse to rotate the cube. A hands-on study of rotation matrices and perspective projection, implemented in TypeScript and rendered with CSS transforms.

Move your mouse over the cube to rotate it. Each of its eight vertices is a `div`; TypeScript computes the rotated coordinates and CSS transforms position the dots.

The DOM rendering is a deliberate constraint that keeps the calculation visible, from matrix multiplication to motion on screen.

## Rotate eight points

A cube has eight vertices. Each vertex is a point in space: $(x, y, z)$.

To rotate the cube, we need new coordinates for every vertex—coordinates that place each point in its rotated position.

Rotation matrices perform that transformation. In this demo, the math is done directly in TypeScript and the result is pushed into CSS transforms.

## One Axis at a Time

Rotation around an axis leaves that axis unchanged. Rotating around $z$ moves points in the $xy$-plane. Rotating around $x$ moves points in the $yz$-plane.

Angles below are in **radians**: a quarter turn is $\pi/2$. Coordinates are multiplied as column vectors, and these are active rotations: points move while the axes stay fixed. The right-hand convention determines each sign, as in Lynch and Park’s [Modern Robotics rotation-matrix explanation](https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/3-2-1-rotation-matrices-part-1-of-2/).

Each axis has its own matrix. In the plane perpendicular to that axis the picture is a 2D rotation: counterclockwise when $y$ points up (the math convention), clockwise when $y$ points down (the screen).

![A coral arrow starting on the x-axis and turning left by an angle theta, with y pointing up.](/images/research/rotation-ccw.svg?v=7)

*θ measured left from +x. This is the usual math picture, with y pointing up.*

![A coral arrow starting on the x-axis and turning right by an angle theta, with y pointing down.](/images/research/rotation-cw.svg?v=7)

*θ measured right from +x. Screens number y downward, so the same matrix looks clockwise.*

### Around X

The first row is $[1, 0, 0]$. This preserves $x$:

$$R_x(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ 0 & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$$

```typescript
const rotationX = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [1, 0, 0],
        [0, Math.cos(angle), -Math.sin(angle)],
        [0, Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle)]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}
```

### Around Y

The middle row is $[0, 1, 0]$. A rotation around the $y$-axis leaves $y$ unchanged while rotating points in the $xz$-plane:

$$R_y(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$$
```typescript
const rotationY = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [Math.cos(angle), 0, Math.sin(angle)],
        [0, 1, 0],
        [-Math.sin(angle), 0, Math.cos(angle)]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}
```

### Around Z

The last row is $[0, 0, 1]$. This preserves $z$:

$$R_z(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

```typescript
const rotationZ = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [Math.cos(angle), -Math.sin(angle), 0],
        [Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle), 0],
        [0, 0, 1]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}
```

## Applying a Rotation

To rotate a vertex, multiply the matrix by its coordinates:

$$\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ z' \end{bmatrix} = R \cdot \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}$$

For example, $R_z(\pi/2)(1,0,0)^T = (0,1,0)^T$: positive $x$ turns to positive $y$. Rotation preserves length; only the later scaling and projection change the on-screen size.

The result $(x', y', z')$ is the rotated position. Do that for every vertex and the whole shape turns. The origin stays put.

![A flat x-y plane. A dashed L sits on the x-axis; a coral L is the same figure turned by theta. The turn arc has an arrow.](/images/research/rotation-apply.svg?v=7)

*Apply R to every corner. Same L, turned by θ. Ghost is before, coral is after.*

In this demo, that math is done in plain TypeScript:
```typescript
const matrixMultiplyVertex = (matrix: number[][], vertex: Vertex): Vertex => {
    const result: number[][] = []
    for (let i = 0; i < matrix.length; i++) {
        let sum = 0
        sum += matrix[i][0] * vertex.x
        sum += matrix[i][1] * vertex.y
        sum += matrix[i][2] * vertex.z
        result[i] = [sum]
    }
    return { x: result[0][0], y: result[1][0], z: result[2][0] }
}
```

## Combining Rotations

The cube above uses all three matrices in sequence: $R_x$, then $R_y$, then $R_z$.

This demo uses **column vectors** and $v' = Mv$ (matrix on the left). Composition is right-to-left: apply $R_x$, then $R_y$, then $R_z$. Rotations are **active** (they move the cube; the axes stay put) and **right-handed**: a positive angle is counterclockwise when you look along the axis toward the origin. Screens flip $y$, so the same $R_z$ looks clockwise on the page. The view step later is not a rotation — it is a projective scale.

Order matters. Rotating first around $z$ then around $x$ is not the same as $x$ then $z$. Matrix multiplication is not commutative. Walk it one turn at a time:

![Step 1. An L lies on the xy plane. Axes x, y, and z meet at the origin.](/images/research/rotation-combine-1.svg?v=7)

*1 · Start. The L sits on the xy plane.*
![Step 2. The L has turned around z. Ghost shows the start pose. The L is still on the floor.](/images/research/rotation-combine-2.svg?v=7)

*2 · Apply Rz. It turns around z and stays on the floor.*

![Step 3. The L from step 2 has now tipped around x. Ghost is the after-Rz pose.](/images/research/rotation-combine-3.svg?v=7)

*3 · Then Rx. That pose tips around x.*
![Step 4. Other order: the L first tipped around x, then turned around z. A coral arrow marks the last turn. The pose does not match step 3.](/images/research/rotation-combine-4.svg?v=7)

*4 · Other order: Rx first, then Rz. Same two turns, different pose.*

![Two coral L poses side by side. Left is Rz then Rx. Right is Rx then Rz. A not-equals sign sits between them.](/images/research/rotation-combine-5.svg?v=7)

*5 · The two finals. Same turns, opposite order — not the same pose.*

A single rotation about an arbitrary axis $\hat{u}$ is the same idea in one step: the part of $\vec{v}$ along $\hat{u}$ is fixed; the rest spins in the plane of $\theta$.

```typescript
export const transformPoints = (
    vertexArray: Vertex[],
    angleX: number,
    angleY: number,
    angleZ: number,
    scale: number,
    eyeDistance: number,
) => {
    let rotatedPoints = rotationX(vertexArray, angleX)
    rotatedPoints = rotationY(rotatedPoints, angleY)
    rotatedPoints = rotationZ(rotatedPoints, angleZ)
    const scaledPoints = scaleXYZ(rotatedPoints, scale)
    return projectPoints(scaledPoints, eyeDistance)
}
```

## From 3D to Screen

After rotation the cube is still in 3D. The screen is 2D.

A ray from the eye through the screen hits the point. Where it crosses the screen is what you draw.

The gap from the eye to the screen is **eye distance** $d$ (the camera's $z$ when the plane sits at $z = 0$). The two triangles — eye to the screen hit, and eye to the point — are the same shape, so **height on screen** is a shrink of **height in space**:

$$\text{height on screen} = \text{height in space} \times \frac{d}{\text{depth}}$$

Depth here is $d - z$. Farther away means a larger depth, so a smaller mark. In coordinates measured from the eye, the same horizontal construction is $B_x = A_x \cdot d / A_z$: $A_z$ then denotes eye-relative depth, rather than the demo's world-space $z$.

![An eye in front of a screen. A coral tree in space spans height in space; its projection on the screen spans height on screen. A ray through both tops. Braces mark d and depth. The equation height on screen = height in space times d over depth sits at the top left.](/images/research/rotation-perspective.svg?v=17)

*Height on screen is a shrink of height in space. Same colors as the braces.*

The demo stores $d$ as `eyeDistance` and uses a normalized **perspective scale** $s = 1/(d - z)$. This omits the fixed numerator $d$ from the screen-plane formula above, giving a different overall scale while retaining the inverse-depth relationship. At the same eye distance, farther points land closer to the centre.

![An eye, a screen, and two same-size coral trees at different depths. Green rays run from the eye to each tree’s top and base. A stacked key marks solid as near and dashed as far. On the screen the near image is large and the far image is small and closer to the middle, both fully on the film. Braces mark d and d minus z.](/images/research/rotation-f-projection.svg?v=16)

*Perspective scale = 1/(d − z). Solid rays = near, dashed = far. Farther away → smaller on the screen, closer to the middle.*

```typescript
const projectPoints = (vertexArray: Vertex[], eyeDistance: number): Vertex[] => {
    const result: Vertex[] = []
    vertexArray.forEach(vertex => {
        const perspectiveScale = 1 / (eyeDistance - vertex.z)
        const projectionMatrix = [
            [perspectiveScale, 0, 0],
            [0, perspectiveScale, 0],
            [0, 0, 1]
        ]
        result.push(matrixMultiplyVertex(projectionMatrix, vertex))
    })
    return result
}
```
For $d=4$, a point with $x=2$ and $z=0$ projects to $x=0.5$; at $z=2$ it projects to $x=1$. The denominator is zero at the eye plane $z=d$, not at the screen plane $z=0$. A robust renderer must clip points before they reach or cross the eye plane; this demo does not implement that clipping.

Each frame, eight vertices become eight screen positions. Those positions render as the dots you see above.

### The Render Loop

React manages the vertices as state. When mouse movement triggers a recalculation, the component re-renders with new coordinates:

```typescript
{vertices.map((vertex, index) => (
    <div
        key={index}
        className={styles.vertex}
        style={{
            // Template literal: backticks allow embedded expressions ${...}
            // to inject computed coordinates directly into the CSS string
            transform: `translate3d(
                ${vertex.x + center.x}px,
                ${vertex.y + center.y}px,
                ${vertex.z}px
            )`
        }}
    />
))}
```

The browser handles the actual positioning. We compute the math; CSS does the rendering.

The browser decides how to composite the transformed elements. This experiment makes the coordinate calculation inspectable; it supplies no GPU-performance measurement or production-rendering comparison.

## The complete code

This reference puts the transformation steps together so they can be read without moving between sections. It is a simplified equivalent of `lib/matrixTransformations.ts`, whose multiplication routine handles matrix dimensions explicitly. Despite its name, `scaleXYZ` scales only $x$ and $y$; $z$ is left unchanged. The final JSX fragment belongs inside the React component, where `vertices`, `styles`, and `center` are supplied. The fragment and functions are not a standalone application.

```typescript
interface Vertex {
    x: number
    y: number
    z: number
}

const rotationX = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [1, 0, 0],
        [0, Math.cos(angle), -Math.sin(angle)],
        [0, Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle)]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}

const rotationY = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [Math.cos(angle), 0, Math.sin(angle)],
        [0, 1, 0],
        [-Math.sin(angle), 0, Math.cos(angle)]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}

const rotationZ = (vertexArray: Vertex[], angle: number): Vertex[] => {
    const rotationMatrix = [
        [Math.cos(angle), -Math.sin(angle), 0],
        [Math.sin(angle), Math.cos(angle), 0],
        [0, 0, 1]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, rotationMatrix)
}

const transformPointsWithMatrix = (vertexArray: Vertex[], matrix: number[][]): Vertex[] => {
    return vertexArray.map(vertex => matrixMultiplyVertex(matrix, vertex))
}

const matrixMultiplyVertex = (matrix: number[][], vertex: Vertex): Vertex => {
    const result: number[][] = []
    for (let i = 0; i < matrix.length; i++) {
        let sum = 0
        sum += matrix[i][0] * vertex.x
        sum += matrix[i][1] * vertex.y
        sum += matrix[i][2] * vertex.z
        result[i] = [sum]
    }
    return { x: result[0][0], y: result[1][0], z: result[2][0] }
}

const scaleXYZ = (vertexArray: Vertex[], scale: number): Vertex[] => {
    const scaleMatrix = [
        [scale, 0, 0],
        [0, scale, 0],
        [0, 0, 1]
    ]
    return transformPointsWithMatrix(vertexArray, scaleMatrix)
}

const projectPoints = (vertexArray: Vertex[], eyeDistance: number): Vertex[] => {
    const result: Vertex[] = []
    vertexArray.forEach(vertex => {
        const perspectiveScale = 1 / (eyeDistance - vertex.z)
        const projectionMatrix = [
            [perspectiveScale, 0, 0],
            [0, perspectiveScale, 0],
            [0, 0, 1]
        ]
        result.push(matrixMultiplyVertex(projectionMatrix, vertex))
    })
    return result
}

export const transformPoints = (
    vertexArray: Vertex[],
    angleX: number,
    angleY: number,
    angleZ: number,
    scale: number,
    eyeDistance: number,
) => {
    let rotatedPoints = rotationX(vertexArray, angleX)
    rotatedPoints = rotationY(rotatedPoints, angleY)
    rotatedPoints = rotationZ(rotatedPoints, angleZ)
    const scaledPoints = scaleXYZ(rotatedPoints, scale)
    return projectPoints(scaledPoints, eyeDistance)
}

{vertices.map((vertex, index) => (
    <div
        key={index}
        className={styles.vertex}
        style={{
            transform: `translate3d(
                ${vertex.x + center.x}px,
                ${vertex.y + center.y}px,
                ${vertex.z}px
            )`
        }}
    />
))}
```
---

### Live Order Book: Real-Time Market Visualization
*Streaming top-of-book depth with WebSockets and React*
Tags: React, TypeScript, WebSocket, Binance API, Data Visualization, Market Microstructure, Cryptocurrency
Summary: An interactive guide to bids, asks, spread, and visible market depth using live Binance WebSocket data
An interactive explainer of bids, asks, spread, and order-book depth using Binance’s public depth stream. A 20-level stream supplies the metrics; the table shows 10 levels per side and the depth chart shows 15.

## What is an Order Book?

In a marketplace, some market participants want to **buy**, and others want to **sell**. An order book records resting buy and sell orders, grouped by price.

Below, the demo attempts to connect to Binance’s partial depth stream through a **WebSocket**, a persistent connection that lets the exchange push updates. It requests 20 price levels on each side at 100 ms intervals, as specified in the [partial-depth stream documentation](https://developers.binance.com/docs/binance-spot-api-docs/web-socket-streams#partial-book-depth-streams). The table displays 10 levels per side, the depth chart displays 15, and metrics use the received 20. Connection failure or unavailable data prevents a current reading.

For BTC/USDT, **BTC** (bitcoin) is the base asset being bought or sold; **USDT** (Tether) is the quote asset in which its price is stated. Prices are USDT per BTC, not US dollars. The demo’s dollar-sign price labels are a display shorthand, not a currency conversion.

## Bids and asks

### Bids (Buy Side)

**Bids** are prices at which traders are willing to buy.

> "Buy 0.5 BTC at 93,000 USDT"

The **best bid** is the highest buy price currently in the book. It defines the top of the bid side.

### Asks (Sell Side)

**Asks** are prices at which traders are willing to sell.

> "Sell 0.3 BTC at 93,050 USDT"

The **best ask** is the lowest sell price currently in the book. It defines the top of the ask side.

Together, best bid and best ask define the **top of book**.

---

## Read the displayed volume and spread

### Order Imbalance

**Order imbalance** compares visible buy and sell volume. In this demo, it reflects the top 20 levels of the book, not the full market.

Displayed volume does not tell us how many traders placed the orders or whether those orders will remain. Imbalance alone does not predict the next price.

#### Where Does Volume Come From?

Every order in the book has a **size**, how many units someone wants to buy or sell at that price.

Here is an invented two-level example in **JSON**, a text format for structured data. For a hypothetical BASE/USDT pair, each inner pair contains price (USDT per BASE), then quantity (BASE units). These numbers are not a BTC snapshot:

```json
{
  "bids": [["2.35", "1500"], ["2.34", "800"]],
  "asks": [["2.36", "1200"], ["2.37", "600"]]
}
```

The first bid level contains 1,500 BASE units at 2.35 USDT per BASE; the first ask level contains 1,200 BASE units at 2.36 USDT per BASE. Quantity is measured in the base asset, as distinguished from quote-asset spending in Binance’s [new-order documentation](https://developers.binance.com/docs/binance-spot-api-docs/rest-api/trading-endpoints#new-order-trade). Each level can aggregate several orders.

**Total volume** is just adding up all the sizes on each side:

- Bids: 1,500 + 800 = **2,300 total**
- Asks: 1,200 + 600 = **1,800 total**

```typescript
const totalBidVolume = bids.reduce((sum, entry) => sum + entry.size, 0)
const totalAskVolume = asks.reduce((sum, entry) => sum + entry.size, 0)
```

#### How Imbalance Is Calculated

The formula compares how much is on each side:

> **Order Imbalance** = (Bid Volume − Ask Volume) ÷ (Bid Volume + Ask Volume)

Subtract ask volume from bid volume, then divide by their combined volume.

```typescript
const orderImbalance = (totalBidVolume - totalAskVolume) / (totalBidVolume + totalAskVolume)
```

For nonzero combined volume, the result lies between -1 and +1. If both sides are empty, the ratio is undefined. The inline card currently substitutes zero for an undefined ratio; that empty-data placeholder must not be interpreted as evidence of a balanced market.

| Result | What It Means |
|--------|---------------|
| **+1** | Bid volume only |
| **+0.5** | Bid volume is three times ask volume |
| **0** | Equal bid and ask volume |
| **-0.5** | Ask volume is three times bid volume |
| **-1** | Ask volume only |

#### A Simple Example

Using the numbers above (bids = 2,300, asks = 1,800):

$$\frac{2300 - 1800}{2300 + 1800} = \frac{500}{4100} = 0.12$$

Rounded to two decimal places, the imbalance is **+0.12**. In the live card’s percentage format, the unrounded ratio would display as **12.20%**. Bid volume exceeds ask volume in these displayed levels.

---

### Spread

The **spread** is the gap between the best ask and the best bid:

> Spread = Best Ask − Best Bid

The live value above shows the current spread for the selected trading pair.

A narrow spread puts the best available buying and selling prices close together. A wider spread increases the gap an immediate trade must cross. Liquidity also depends on how much size is available at those prices and farther into the book.

---

### Market Depth

The colored bars aggregate **volume at each price level**. Longer bars mean more resting size at that price.

Depth shows where displayed size is concentrated and which price levels an immediate order may consume. This partial view cannot account for orders beyond the displayed levels or changes before execution.

---

## How Trades Execute

A buy can execute when its price condition permits matching an available sell, and conversely for a sell. The following is a simplified execution model; the displayed depth is neither a trade instruction nor a guarantee of execution.

Two basic order types:

1. **Market order**  
   - “Buy now, whatever the best available price is.”  
   - Attempts to match against available prices on the opposite side; the price is not guaranteed.
   - Consumes liquidity.

2. **Limit order**  
   - “Buy at 93,000 or better (lower).”  
   - Can execute immediately if it crosses an available price.
   - An unfilled portion supplies resting liquidity only if the order’s conditions allow it.

When a market buy arrives, it lifts the lowest ask.  
When a market sell arrives, it hits the highest bid.  
A large order may consume several price levels and receive several execution prices. A **partial fill** means only part of the requested quantity executed. Binance’s [time-in-force and order-status definitions](https://developers.binance.com/docs/binance-spot-api-docs/enums#time-in-force-timeinforce) distinguish orders that may rest until cancelled (GTC), those that cancel an unfilled remainder immediately (IOC), and those requiring a complete immediate fill (FOK). Orders can expire after a partial fill; visible liquidity can also change before execution.
